# Torticollis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Spine > Torticollis*

[Original Article Link](/library/kQ0mwf)

---

## Summary

Torticollis (wryneck) is a postural deformity characterized by head tilt and/or neck rotation. Torticollis may be congenital, acquired, or <u>idiopathic</u>. The diagnostic workup and treatment of torticollis vary based on the presence of <u>red flags for torticollis</u> and the suspected underlying etiology. <u>Congenital muscular torticollis</u> (<u>CMT</u>), the most common type of <u>congenital torticollis</u>, may present with palpable abnormalities of the <u>sternocleidomastoid</u> (SCM) muscle, such as thickening, tightening, and/or mass. <u>CMT</u> generally does not require diagnostic studies and is <u>managed conservatively</u>, e.g., with <u>physical therapy</u>; refractory cases may require diagnostic studies, <u>botulinum toxin</u> injections, or <u>surgery</u>. For nonmuscular <u>congenital torticollis</u> (e.g., due to bony abnormalities) and <u>acquired torticollis</u> (e.g., due to muscular, neurologic, bony, and ocular abnormalities), clinical features of the underlying etiology may be present, and management is aimed at addressing the underlying cause.

---

## Types of torticollis

* Congenital torticollis [[1]](/library/vuWAGM0)

* Develops prenatally

* ∼ 80% of cases are due to <u>CMT</u>, a contraction of the SCM muscle.   [[1]](/library/vuWAGM0)[[2]](/library/zadrMo0)

* Causes of nonmuscular <u>congenital torticollis</u> include bony abnormalities and neck masses.

* See “<u>Congenital torticollis</u>” for additional information.

* <u>Acquired torticollis</u> [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)

* Develops after <u>birth</u> and has an identifiable cause

* See “<u>Acquired torticollis</u>” for additional information.

* <u>Idiopathic torticollis</u>  [[4]](/library/c9XamZ0)[[5]](/library/pYdLJo0)

* Develops after <u>birth</u> and does not have an identifiable cause

* Age of onset: ∼ 50 years [[4]](/library/c9XamZ0)

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (2:1) [[4]](/library/c9XamZ0)

* See “<u>Dystonia</u>” for additional information.

---

## Congenital muscular torticollis

### Etiology  [[1]](/library/vuWAGM0)[[3]](/library/WJXPG_)[[9]](/library/NuW-rM0)




* Prenatal intrauterine malpositioning or constraint, e.g., from

* <u>Breech presentation</u>

* <u>Multiple gestation</u>

* <u>Oligohydramnios</u>

* <u>Macrosomia</u>

* SCM injury during <u>birth</u>: <u>hematoma</u> → <u>fibrosis</u> and/or <u>contracture</u> → unilateral shortening of the SCM

* Abnormal development, <u>hypertrophy</u>, or unilateral absence of an SCM muscle





### Clinical features [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)[[8]](/library/y-Wd-L0)




* Head tilt or postural preference  

* May not appear until 2–8 weeks of age  [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)

* The head is tilted toward the contracted SCM with <u>contralateral</u> chin rotation.  [[8]](/library/y-Wd-L0)

* Limited passive <u>ROM</u> and, in more severe cases, limited active <u>ROM</u>  [[9]](/library/NuW-rM0)

* SCM thickening, tightening, and/or palpable mass (findings differ by severity)  [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)

* Associated abnormalities are common, e.g., [[2]](/library/zadrMo0)[[8]](/library/y-Wd-L0)

* Craniofacial asymmetry

* <u>Foot deformities</u> (e.g., <u>clubfoot</u>, <u>metatarsus adductus</u>)

* <u>Developmental hip dysplasia</u>

* <u>Developmental delay</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Congenital muscular torticollis</u> most commonly affects the right SCM muscle. [[8]](/library/y-Wd-L0)




![Congenital muscular torticollis](media/qup38w4yq4pgbrxv3p46zx19.jpg)

Congenital muscular torticollis




### Diagnostics [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)[[6]](/library/VYdGLo0)[[8]](/library/y-Wd-L0)




Diagnostic studies are not indicated for most <u>infants</u> with suspected <u>CMT</u>. [[9]](/library/NuW-rM0)




* Indications for imaging

* <u>Red flags for torticollis</u>

* Suspected nonmuscular <u>congenital torticollis</u>

* <u>Neonates</u>

* Persistent symptoms despite <u>physical therapy</u>

* Modalities

* <u>Ultrasound</u> <u>cervical spine</u>: initial evaluation in <u>neonates</u> and for persistent <u>CMT</u>  [[1]](/library/vuWAGM0)

* <u>X-ray cervical spine</u> (AP and <u>lateral</u>) or CT neck: for suspected bony abnormalities [[7]](/library/JuWsHM0)

* <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> and neck: for suspected <u>CNS</u> causes





### Differential diagnosis




* Nonmuscular <u>congenital torticollis</u> [[9]](/library/NuW-rM0)

* Etiology

* Bony abnormalities (e.g., <u>cervical spine</u> <u>scoliosis</u>, <u>hemivertebra</u>, <u>Sprengel deformity</u>, <u>Klippel-Feil syndrome</u>)

* <u>Congenital neck masses</u> (e.g., <u>branchial cleft cyst</u>, <u>cystic hygroma</u>, SCM cyst)

* <u>Pterygium colli</u> (<u>webbed neck</u>)

* Clinical features: in addition to head tilt, clinical features of the underlying etiology may be present.

* Management: Refer to the appropriate specialist  for treatment of the underlying cause.

* <u>Acquired torticollis</u>: e.g., <u>Sandifer syndrome</u>, <u>benign paroxysmal torticollis of infancy</u>, <u>ocular torticollis</u>





### Management [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)[[9]](/library/NuW-rM0)




The following recommendations are for patients with <u>CMT</u>.




* Promptly refer to <u>physical therapy</u>.  [[1]](/library/vuWAGM0)[[7]](/library/JuWsHM0)

* Educate caregivers on: [[9]](/library/NuW-rM0)

* Home passive stretching exercises

* Supervised <u>tummy time</u>

* Passive positioning of the <u>infant</u>

* Refractory symptoms: Consider specialist referral for procedural therapy, e.g.: [[1]](/library/vuWAGM0)[[7]](/library/JuWsHM0)

* <u>Botulinum toxin</u> injection

* <u>Surgery</u> (e.g., myotomy, bipolar <u>tenotomy</u>): may be indicated if symptoms persist past 12 months of age  [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)





> [!WARNING]
> Do not delay referral to <u>physical therapy</u>. Earlier intervention increases success rates and decreases the need for invasive interventions. [[9]](/library/NuW-rM0)




### Complications [[10]](/library/xedEa60)




* Craniofacial asymmetry (e.g., positional plagiocephaly)

* <u>Scoliosis</u> of the <u>cervical spine</u>

## Acquired torticollis

### Etiology




| <br>Etiology of <u>acquired torticollis</u> [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)[[8]](/library/y-Wd-L0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
|  | Causes |
| Muscular (due to cervical muscle spasms) | <br><br>* <u>Neck sprain</u> or <u>neck strain</u> from:<br><br>* Injury or overuse<br><br>* Poor <u>sleep</u> position<br><br>* Drug-induced <u>acute dystonic reaction</u> from <u>dopamine</u>-<u>receptor</u> <u>antagonists</u> (e.g., <u>haloperidol</u>, <u>chlorpromazine</u>, <u>prochlorperazine</u>, and <u>metoclopramide</u>) [[11]](/library/JYdsJo0)[[12]](/library/qYdCJo0)<br><br><br> |
| Skeletal | <br><br>* <u>Vertebral fractures</u><br><br>* <u>Atlantoaxial subluxation</u> (e.g., due to trauma or <u>Grisel syndrome</u>)<br><br>* Inflammatory <u>arthritis</u><br><br>* Bone <u>tumor</u> [[6]](/library/VYdGLo0)<br><br><br> |
| Infection | <br><br>* <u>Upper respiratory tract infection</u><br><br>* <u>Retropharyngeal abscess</u><br><br>* Cervical <u>vertebral osteomyelitis</u><br><br>* <u>Cervical lymphadenitis</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>CNS</u> | <br><br>* Neurological injury from <u>birth trauma</u> (e.g., in <u>infants</u> with <u>macrosomia</u>, <u>assisted vaginal delivery</u>)<br><br>* <u>Cerebellar</u> and <u>posterior</u> fossae lesions<br><br>* Cervical <u>spinal cord lesions</u>  and <u>nerve root</u> irritation<br><br>* <u>Cervical spine injury</u>, including <u>spinal cord compression</u> and <u>spinal epidural hematoma</u><br><br>* <u>Cerebral palsy</u> [[8]](/library/y-Wd-L0)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Ocular torticollis (a compensatory head position to maintain binocularity) [[7]](/library/JuWsHM0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Strabismus</u><br><br>* <u>Nystagmus</u> (e.g., <u>spasmus nutans</u>)<br><br>* <u>Cranial nerve IV palsy</u><br><br>* <u>Refractive errors</u><br><br><br> |
| Other causes | <br><br>* <u>GERD</u> in association with <u>Sandifer syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Benign paroxysmal torticollis of infancy</u> [[7]](/library/JuWsHM0)<br><br><br> |





### Clinical features [[6]](/library/VYdGLo0)




* Acquired muscular torticollis

* Spontaneous onset; may occur overnight without provocation [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)

* Head tilt <u>ipsilateral</u> to the muscle spasm with <u>contralateral</u> chin rotation   [[8]](/library/y-Wd-L0)

* Limited cervical <u>ROM</u>

* SCM <u>pain</u> and tightness

* <u>Acute dystonic reaction</u>: other <u>extrapyramidal symptoms</u>

* Acquired nonmuscular torticollis

* Features of the underlying cause

* See “<u>Red flags for torticollis</u>.”





![Torticollis](media/xrv6ho5fqrxo48116x5upxtz.jpg)

Torticollis




### Diagnostics [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)[[6]](/library/VYdGLo0)[[8]](/library/y-Wd-L0)




* No <u>red flags for torticollis</u>: diagnostic studies not routinely required

* <u>Red flags for torticollis</u> present: Obtain diagnostic studies based on suspected underlying cause.

* Infection: <u>CBC with differential</u>, cultures, <u>inflammatory markers</u>

* Osseous emergencies: <u>X-ray cervical spine</u>, CT neck

* Neurological emergencies: <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> and neck, CT neck





### Treatment [[3]](/library/WJXPG_)[[8]](/library/y-Wd-L0)




Treatment is based on the underlying condition; involve appropriate specialists as needed.




#### Muscular torticollis




Acquired muscular torticollis is typically <u>self-limiting</u> with resolution in 7–10 days. Treatment is mainly conservative.




* Soft <u>cervical collar</u>

* Passive and active stretching exercises

* Localized heat, massage

* <u>NSAIDs</u>  or <u>muscle relaxants</u>  [[13]](/library/9edNa60)

* Refractory symptoms: See “<u>Cervical dystonia</u>.”





#### Drug-induced <u>acute dystonic reaction</u> [[14]](/library/8YdOIo0)




* Stop offending agent.

* Initiate IV <u>anticholinergics</u> (e.g., <u>benztropine</u>, <u>diphenhydramine</u>).

* See “<u>Acute dystonia</u>.”





#### <u>Ocular torticollis</u> [[7]](/library/JuWsHM0)




* Treatment depends on the underlying cause.

* Options include <u>eye</u> patches, glasses, and/or <u>extraocular muscle</u> <u>surgery</u>.
